teaser: Autumn fruit on an Easter table, and a basket about to fall into your lap.
review_notes:
Payment of 150 scudi by Ciriaco Mattei in January 1602: check amount and date.
Bellori's complaints (1672) about the out-of-season fruit, the beardless Christ and the innkeeper's cap: paraphrased, not quoted.
Identification of the left disciple as Cleopas follows tradition; the Gospel names only one of the two.
The 'fish-shaped' shadow of the basket is a modern observation, not a documented intention.
National Gallery acquisition in 1839 (gift of Lord Vernon): check.

lesson.text: The story happens three days after the Crucifixion, so at Easter, in early spring. Now check the basket on the table: grapes, figs, a split pomegranate, apples with wormholes. Those are the fruits of September. Caravaggio set an autumn harvest on a spring table, and people noticed.

One early biographer, Bellori, listed it among the painter's faults, along with a few others we will meet. But the contradiction tells you how Caravaggio worked. He painted what he could put in front of him in his studio. If the basket in the room was full of autumn fruit, autumn fruit went into the Gospel.

The Gospel of Luke gives the plot. Two disciples walk to the village of Emmaus, crushed by the death of Jesus. A stranger joins them on the road. They invite him to eat. At the table he blesses the bread, and in that second they understand who he is. Then he vanishes.
Caravaggio paints the half second of recognition: after the blessing has begun, before anyone has had time to speak.

lesson.title: Three men, three reactions
lesson.text: Everyone at the table receives the same gesture. Nobody takes it the same way.

spots.title: The man who jumps
spots.text: Seen from behind, he grips the arm of his chair and starts to rise. His green jacket is torn at the elbow, a white patch of shirt showing through. These are poor men.

spots.title: The man who opens his arms
spots.text: Arms flung wide, as wide as a cross. The scallop shell pinned to his chest was the badge of pilgrims, travelers on a holy road.

spots.title: The man who sees nothing
spots.text: The innkeeper, cap still on his head, thumbs in his belt. He watches his customers get excited and has no idea why. He is looking at the miracle and missing it.

lesson.text: That standing innkeeper is the one figure you might overlook, and he is the one closest to most of us: present, attentive, and not understanding. Bellori counted his cap as bad manners in front of Christ. But the man does not know it is Christ. His ignorance is the point.
Caravaggio was about 30 and the most talked-about painter in Rome when the nobleman Ciriaco Mattei ordered this picture. The account books record a payment of 150 scudi in January 1602.
Now the face in the middle. For more than a thousand years, painters had given the risen Christ long hair and a beard. So why did two men who had followed him for months fail to know him on the road?
What is missing from the face of Christ that almost every other painting gives him?

spots.title: No beard
spots.text: A smooth, full, young face. The Gospel of Mark says the risen Jesus appeared “in another form”. Caravaggio takes it literally: the disciples did not recognize him because he looked different.

lesson.text: So the second “mistake” is an answer. A beardless Christ explains the plot. It also unsettled viewers who expected the familiar face, and it makes you work the way the disciples do: you identify him by what he does with his hand, not by how he looks.

The size matters here. The canvas is about 141 by 196 cm (roughly 4.6 by 6.4 feet), so the figures are life size and cut off at the waist by the table. You stand where a fourth guest would sit. And Caravaggio keeps pushing things out of the picture toward that empty seat.
Three things break through the surface of the painting and come at you.

lines.label: The arms
lines.text: One hand is far back near Christ, the other huge and close, almost touching the edge. The stretch of these arms measures the depth of the room in a single gesture.

lines.label: The blessing
lines.text: Christ's arm is foreshortened, meaning drawn as if pointing straight toward you so it looks shortened. The hand ends up in front of the table, in your space.

lines.label: The basket
lines.text: The fruit basket hangs over the front edge of the table. One nudge and it lands on the floor at your feet. It is a way of making you want to reach in.

lesson.text: None of this would work without the light. It falls from high on the left, as if from a single window, and leaves the rest in near blackness. This strong contrast of light and dark has a name, chiaroscuro, and Caravaggio made it the fashion of a generation.

The light also plays a quiet trick. The innkeeper stands between the source and Christ, and his shadow darkens the wall behind. Yet Christ's face stays fully lit. The shadow frames the head like a dark halo, without any gold disk being painted.

Caravaggio made no preparatory drawings that we know of. He posed models in the studio and painted straight onto the canvas, sometimes scoring guide lines into the wet ground with the handle of his brush.
The table itself is worth a slow visit. A still life is a painting of objects, usually food or flowers, and here Caravaggio tucks one of the finest of his career into a religious scene.

spots.title: The basket
spots.text: Grapes, a pomegranate, pears and apples with spots and bruises. The fruit is ripe to the point of decay, painted blemish by blemish.

spots.title: The shadow
spots.text: On the white cloth, the basket throws a sharp shadow. Some viewers see the shape of a fish in it, an old Christian sign. Nothing proves the painter meant it.

spots.title: Water and wine
spots.text: A glass carafe and a glass catch the light, and cast bright reflections on the cloth instead of plain shadows. Bread and wine recall the Mass.

spots.title: The fowl
spots.text: A roast bird, legs in the air. Plain inn food, painted with the same attention as the sacred hand above it.

spots.title: The other hand
spots.text: Christ's left hand hovers above the bread, between resting and blessing.

spots.title: The carpet
spots.text: Under the white linen lies a patterned Eastern rug, a luxury in Rome. The inn is humble, the table is dressed like an altar.

lesson.text: The painting later belonged to Cardinal Scipione Borghese, the greediest collector in Rome. It reached London in the 19th century and has hung in the National Gallery since 1839.

Five years after this picture, Caravaggio killed a man in a street fight and fled Rome. On the run, he painted the supper at Emmaus again. That second version, now in Milan, has no flung arms and almost no fruit. Christ is bearded, tired, half in shadow. Same story, told by a man who no longer felt like showing off.

quiz.question: What is odd about the fruit basket?
options: It holds autumn fruit although the scene takes place at Easter
It contains fruit unknown in Italy
quiz.explanation: Grapes, figs and pomegranates ripen in autumn, not in spring.

quiz.question: Why is Christ shown without a beard?
options: To explain why the disciples did not recognize him
The patron demanded a portrait of his son
quiz.explanation: Mark's Gospel says he appeared in another form.

quiz.question: What does the scallop shell on the right-hand disciple mean?
quiz.explanation: The shell was the badge worn by pilgrims.

quiz.question: Who fails to understand what is happening?
quiz.explanation: He keeps his cap on and simply watches.

quiz.question: What is chiaroscuro?
options: Strong contrast between light and dark
quiz.explanation: Caravaggio made this dramatic lighting famous.

quiz.question: How does the later version in Milan differ?
options: It is larger and more crowded
It is quieter, darker, with a bearded Christ
quiz.explanation: Painted in flight, it drops the grand gestures.

facts.text: The figures in the painting are about life size.
facts.explanation: The canvas measures roughly 141 by 196 cm, so the half-length figures match a real person.

facts.text: The innkeeper has removed his cap out of respect for Christ.
facts.explanation: He keeps it on because he has not understood who his guest is.

facts.text: Caravaggio painted the subject only once.
facts.explanation: He painted a second, much calmer version about five years later.
